utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and to everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Tecla Henry-Benjamin, Mathias Neuner, Stefan Waespi, Daryl Mundis, and our case manager, Janet Stewart. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Could we have the appearances for Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, and Alexis Demirdjian, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the appearances for the other Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber greets everyone present. Today on the 19th of January, I greet all the representatives of the Prosecution, who are present. I greet Defence counsel, though one member of Defence counsel is missing; as well as the other Defence team. I also greet everyone else in the courtroom and those who are around the courtroom and providing us with assistance. We will be resuming with our work today, and we will be hearing a witness who I expect is ready to testify. I will now ask the usher to call the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we have a technical problem. Our computer with the LiveNote is not functioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we try to deal with this technical problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apart from the technical problem with the computer, can we continue working?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Good day, sir. You have been called as a witness for the Defence. I would first like to make sure that you are receiving the interpretation of what I am saying into your own language. If so, please say that you can hear and understand me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please tell me your first and last names, your date of birth, and your place of birth so that this can be entered into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Mustafa Poparic. I was born on the 30th of September, 1942 in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What current position do you hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, did you hold a position of any kind? And if you were in the army, what sort of assignment did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a member of the Territorial Defence until 1991. I then retired for a few months, and as of April 1992 I was in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, also in the Territorial Defence in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You remained in the Territorial Defence or at any point in time were you assigned to an ABiH unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In November 1992, when the 3rd Corps was formed, I moved over to the corps command, and that is where I finished my career. Because in 1992 and 1993, the Territorial Defence was disbanded and ceased to function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Defence counsel will further clarify the nature of your position within the 3rd Corps when it commences with its examination-in-chief. Have you already testified before an international or a national court with regard to the events that took place in your country in 1992 and 1993, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I'll be testifying before a court of any kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please read out the solemn declaration that the usher will show to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to Defence counsel, who will start with their examination-in-chief, I'd like to provide you with some information about the procedure we'll be following. You'll be testifying this morning about the events that took place in your country in 1992 and 1993. You will have to answer questions put to you by Defence counsel, who are to your left, and whom you have certainly met -- whom you certainly meant before this hearing. After this stage has been completed, the members of the Prosecution, who are very numerous today - they're sitting to your right - will conduct their cross-examination. They will have the same amount of time to ask you questions as the Defence. You will notice that the questions are of a different kind. Defence counsel may not put leading questions to you; however, the Prosecution when conducting its cross-examination may put leading questions to you. After this stage has been completed, Defence counsel may put additional questions to you if they so wish. These questions will directly or indirectly relate to the questions put to you by the Prosecution. After the parties have examined you, the Judges, if they believe it is necessary, may also put questions to you. Sometimes they ask witnesses questions and sometimes they do not. The questions put to you by the Judges are put to witnesses in the interest of justice in order to determine the truth. The Judges may ask you to clarify certain issues raised in the course of your testimony, or the Judges may ask you for your opinion on certain documents that have already been admitted, or the Judges may ask you about statements that have already been made and that seem to contradict your testimony. Generally speaking, this is the procedure we will be following. I should also add that after the Judges have put their questions to you, the parties may take the floor again, ask you additional questions and ask you additional questions that relate to the Judges' questions. There is an adversarial debate that concerns the answers you have provided to all the parties concerned. As you were a member of the military, I should also point out that Defence counsel or the Prosecution might present you with certain documents to ask you about your opinion of the documents or to ask you to Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond comment on the document. This is a possibility that may arise. If you find that a question is too complicated, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it, because we don't have any written documents concerning your testimony. This is why your testimony -- your oral testimony, which is transcribed, is important. When assessing the probative weight of your testimony, we'll be relying on the transcript. On the monitor that you have before you, you will see the English transcript of your testimony. I should also mention two other points referred to in our Rules: You have solemnly declared to speak the truth, which means that you should not give false testimony. False testimony is a punishable offence and could be punished by a prison sentence. The Judges will assess the circumstances which false testimony might appear. I should also point out that when you answer a question, you have the right to refuse to answer the question. All witnesses have this right. Why? Because in certain cases the answer might be used to prosecute the witness at a subsequent date. In such exceptional circumstances, the Judges may compel the witness to answer the question, but we guarantee that what you say will not be used against you at a subsequent date. This provision exists to ensure that the truth can be established, but so far we have never had such a case. If you encounter any difficulties, don't hesitate to inform us of the fact. We are here to deal with any difficulties. As this is the first time you'll be testifying, it might be stressful. But as both parties will act in a courteous manner, I'm sure that your testimony will proceed smoothly. I'll now give the floor to Defence counsel, who will commence with their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Poparic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Presiding Judge has just provided you with a lot of information on the procedure we will be following. I would also like to add that as we speak the same language, you might want to answer the questions I put to you immediately. But as it is necessary for my questions and your answers to be interpreted so that the Chamber and my colleagues can follow our exchanges, I would be grateful if you could make a brief pause after I have put my question to you and then answer the question. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Poparic, you said that you worked in the Municipal TO Staff in Zenica up until 1992. What are you by profession and where were you educated?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I'm a teacher of national defence, I graduated from the University of Political Science in Sarajevo. The People's Defence Department was the department I was in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, before the war, did you have a rank of any kind? And if so, what was your rank? And before you retired, did you have a rank, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I was a reserve major, a member of the artillery, and I worked in the field of organisation and mobilisation throughout the period that I was a member of the Territorial Defence, which was for about 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before you retired, did you have a rank in the ABiH? Or, in fact, what is your rank today or what rank do you have today?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I am a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have just said that you were involved in organisation, mobilisation, and personnel affairs in the Territorial Defence before the war. You also said that you're retired. After the JNA and the Army of Republika Srpska attacked Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 6th of April, in what way did your status as a pensioner change?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Well, just like most of the inhabitants of Zenica, I reported to the Territorial Defence Staff immediately. I wanted to help my people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what assignment were you given in the Territorial Defence Staff?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I was also involved in organisational and mobilisation matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you're performing organisation and mobilisation duties in the TO Staff, did you have any problems as far as mobilising people in wartime conditions was concerned?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Well, in Zenica, we didn't have major problems because you couldn't feel the beginning of the war in Zenica to the same extent as in other areas. So we had a lot of time and a lot of men at our disposal. So we mobilised the first units, made them active in accordance with the plans that we had already prepared.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, at that time in Zenica, in addition to the mobilisation carried out in accordance with the previously prepared plans, were other units that hadn't previously been planned also rapidly formed? And what was your attitude in the Municipal Staff towards such a phenomenon, if it did occur?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everyone was trying to form units of some kind. Every building or every hamlet was trying to do this. For a certain period of time this was under control. But there were also units that were established without having any contact with the TO. They more or less wanted to be independent and there were a number of such units at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, which body in fact dealt with all matters concerning defence and appointed commanders and other officers in the Municipal Staff and formed units and took military decisions on engaging units?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: According to the Law on National Defence that was valid before the war, the Territorial Defence was linked to civilian authorities. The Municipal Staff was under the administrative bodies in the municipality. So initially at the beginning of 1992, there was the War Presidency and the Crisis Staff, and these are the two bodies that would take all the relevant decisions, including decisions on professional matters, expert matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that in Zenica some other organised military units started appearing as a result of the efforts made by various powerful individuals. Can you remember which units refused to recognise the command of the Municipal Staff in the course of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: There were the two components of the Croatian army, the HVO and the HOS; the Muslim Armed Forces; the Green League. There were a number of such units that acted independently. They recognised the Municipal Staff when it was necessary to receive something from the staff, when they needed logistics. But as far as command is concerned, they didn't recognise our command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time in 1992 when a radical change took place in the way military structures were organised within the armed forces in Zenica? And if so, please tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, there was a large number of units in Zenica. At one point, I think there were over a hundred. It was impossible to organise command and control. When I arrived, I tried to have larger units established; however, the watershed was the forming of the corps. This was when brigades were formed and larger units were established instead of the many small ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, please tell us, did you continue to perform the same duty in the Territorial Defence Staff or were you given a new duty when the corps was formed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Well, of course the corps needed personnel, and as I had experience in this kind of work, in mid-November I was transferred from the Municipal Staff to the corps command, performing the same duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your organ, the organ for organisation and mobilisation, who was its superior? Who was your immediate superior and to whom were you linked in the command?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: These matters are linked to the Chief of Staff. My immediate superior was Zijad Bahtic. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that brigades were established at the same time as the corps. From where were men mobilised into the brigades?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: For the most part, this was creating larger units out of small ones. We had platoons, companies, detachments, and then larger detachments of battalion strength were formed. As larger and larger units were established, brigades were formed. There was the 1st Zenica Brigade, and this was mobilised according to the existing pre-war plans, with lower manpower levels to be sure, but according to the same plans. Also, there were many volunteers in Zenica, so we did have manpower at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, you said that you had worked on these affairs for over 30 years. What was the duty of this organ in the corps? What was your main duty in the organ called the organ for organisation, mobilisation, and personnel?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in the corps command, I said that the situation in other municipalities was similar. There were many small units that were difficult to control. The first task of our service was to gain an insight into the existing situation in the municipalities and what the possibilities were for creating larger units out of smaller ones and to make proposals to this effect to the commander. The personnel policy was also within our competence, so that we proposed to the commander the appointments of various people to various duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who prepared proposals for the commander to be submitted to the superior command for appointments within its competence and the reorganisation of certain units?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to proposals coming from other towns, other Municipal Staffs, we made proposals. Part of the commanding officers were appointed by us. I'm not sure any more, but I think it was up to the rank of major. Battalion commanders and ranks above major and colonel, they were appointed by the superior command, and the Presidency appointed higher-ranking officers. We made these proposals in agreement with the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you took up your duty in this service, did you have any records? And what efforts did you make to establish records for the units and the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Initially there were no records. We didn't even know what all the units were. During 1993, we made a great effort to try to create records of the fighters in the 3rd Corps. It was very difficult because the habit wasn't there. Communications were such that we could not obtain regular reports. Entire groups of soldiers moved from one unit another unit. This unit was established, but we couldn't rely on it too much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In order to survey the situation, as far as units and manpower and commands went, were subordinate units duty-bound to supply you with information about their establishment and their manpower levels, and in view of the problems you have set out, did you monitor this by visiting the troops on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, we visited almost all the units in order to gain an insight into the situation as far as manpower levels went and in order to assist these units to set themselves up establishment-wise properly. There were also reports in which they informed us of their numbers, the number of casualties, men moving over from one unit to another. But we could not rely on such data too much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, as the units were formed according to a certain establishment, in 1993 were there major or minor deviations from the manpower levels provided for in the establishment?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had men. We were able to raise all the units up to manpower level, but we did not have sufficient weapons or logistical support, which is why the units were not fully -- were not complete, and they didn't have sufficient manpower.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, for how long did you stay in the command of the 3rd Corps doing this job?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Until November 1993, I performed these tasks in the corps command. After that, pursuant to orders, I became commander of the District Staff of the civilian protection, because the civilian protection was being established in the municipalities and all this had to be linked up and made to function. I stayed there for a year, and after that I returned to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the General Staff, did you do the same job, or were you given other tasks?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I worked in the same service. I worked on the creation of wartime formations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, would you now please show the witness some documents and have the documents distributed to Their Honours and our learned friends and the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, would you please now look at the document issued by the staff of the Supreme Command of the 23rd of July, 1993. And its number is P202. The first thing I wish to ask you is: This document mentions the name of Sakib Mahmuljin. Do you know Mr. Sakib Mahmuljin?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me: In this period of time, was Mr. Sakib Mahmuljin a member of the 3rd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmuljin arrived in Zenica and introduced himself to us, and we accepted him as such. He said he was a representative of the armed forces Supreme Command Staff and that he was there to help us. Therefore, Sakib Mahmuljin was not a member of the command. He lived and worked with us, but officially he was not a member of the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was he employed in the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: No. No, he wasn't an employee of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was he a member of the command of the 3rd Corps? And had he been a member, would you in your command have received an order appointing him to a duty in the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, we would have, because all such orders were kept in our service. Such a document would have had to have been with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that he occasionally came to the corps. Was there a time when he was given a certain duty in the corps? And as far as you can recall, when was this?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Later on, he was appointed Chief of Staff. I think this was in the second half of 1993, August, September, thereabouts, but not until that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I now wish to ask you whether you have ever seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I saw this document for the first time when Mr. Mahmuljin arrived and ordered me to try and set up an establishment, that is, to form a unit which was supposed to soldierise, so to speak, these Arabs who were allegedly on the territory of the 3rd Corps. He showed me this authorisation, and they tried to work on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I hate to interrupt. We are now talking about the first document, not P202, but the second document. Just for the record, if it could be indicated which Prosecution exhibit we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. We were speaking of the document called "Authorisation," numbered P202. This is the first document we talked about. If it is erroneously entered into the transcript, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, before you you had the document issued by the armed forces Supreme Command Staff of the 23rd of July, 1993. Is this the document you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now please look at the next document. This is document numbered - excuse me for a moment - P438. This is document P438. You have just said that Mr. Mahmuljin brought this authorisation to you and told you to make a proposal as to the creation of a formation. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Tell me please, did Mr. Mahmuljin provide you with any elements on the basis of which you would draw up a proposal for this formation?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: When drawing this document, the only thing I knew about was this village of Mehurici. He said they were concentrated there for the most part and he told me what the name of the unit would be. It would be the El Mujahedin Detachment. Had I know what their numbers were, their groupings, locations and so on when drawing up this proposal, I would have mentioned those. I knew of no other elements. The most important information when setting up a formation are the numbers of the men. I didn't know that, so I had to do this off the top of my head without using any elements that I needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, until that time, did you know that there were groups, formations, or individuals who were foreigners in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: We all knew there were some sort of Arabs, but what they were, where they were, how many there were, we really didn't know. I saw them about town in Zenica. They created problems for us in town. But in the units that we registered, there were no such individuals. When I started drawing up this document, that was the first time I learned where they were concentrated and that they were to be part of our army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who gave you these elements, the elements we find here that they are volunteers in the ABiH army, that they are in the village of Mehurici and so on? Did you find this in your records or did you learn these elements from Mr. Mahmuljin?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I learned them from Mr. Mahmuljin because I and the corps command had no record of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Poparic, the initials at the bottom, what do they represent? In the corner.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: "PM PM." The first "PM," these are my initials. It means that I drafted this document in handwriting. The other set of initials refers to the typist who typed the document out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When drafting the document in handwriting, did you refer to the basis on which the person asking you to draw up the document had the right to ask you to do it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Of course, when I started drawing up this proposal, he showed me his authorisation and I mentioned this in the preamble, that this is pursuant to an authorisation by the Supreme Commander, that Mr. Mahmuljin is authorised to contact us, and the information I drew up was based on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, since you have told us that you were involved in similar, identical affairs for about 30 year, tell me: When a commander hands over proposals to form units for the superior command, is it necessary for him to have authorisation to do this?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Well, the commander by virtue of being a commander doesn't require authorisation of any kind. A commander may form any kind of unit and issue such orders without any authorisation in his zone of responsibility because I don't know who would have given him such authorisation. By virtue of his position as a commander, he has the authority to issue such orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, at the bottom of the document - and you said that you wrote it by hand and then handed it over for typing - you can see the name of Commander Enver Hadzihasanovic. How is it that a document for which someone else handles the authorisation and someone else asked you to draft this document, how is it that this document contains a reference to the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: It was quite usual - I think this is normal- that all documents that were going to other parties from the Supreme Command -- from the corps command, all such documents would be authorised or certified by the commander. So everything that we did, any proposals that we drafted, any issues that we -- any orders that we issued, on all such documents we would mark down the name of the commander and hand it over -- hand the documents over to the commander so that he could examine them. Why it hasn't been signed, I don't know. It was probably forwarded by packet communications. I don't know whether it was sent to be signed or not, but we had to draft the document, hand it over to be typed out, and that was the end of my duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who in fact signed this document and do you know whether the corps commander saw this document?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that. I ask for the document to be typed out. I provide it to the relevant body. And it's then their duplicate to take the document to be signed, to inform those who have to be informed about it. That's not my duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, would you please have a look at the next document now, P439. This is an order from the Supreme Command Staff dated the 13th of August, 1993. Do you have that document before you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, after you had drafted this proposal, did you at any time receive this order in your service?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, naturally we did receive this order. I remember the order. This order is in fact a response to the proposal that we had made.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you worked in this field, tell me, according to the rules, who determined the establishment of the newly formed units?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: The Supreme Command was responsible for all wartime establishments.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Supreme Command have to add information on -- on establishment matters to units when it forwarded orders to them?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at item number 1 in the order. Have a look at the paragraph after -- under "Formation," and the sentence where it says, "To form in a 3rd Corps zone of responsibility, the El Mujahedin detachment, according to proposed establishment, which it must submit to the staff for approval." Tell me, does this mean that this military rule is not being respected or were such things things that happened?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Well, the rule wasn't respected here because we received all the information from them, and I assume that they did not have a sufficient number of elements to form such a -- a unit. They assumed that we had more information and that we could draft a proposal that they would then certify or amend. They suggested that we make a suggestion on what we wanted to happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me whether you acted on the basis of this order and did you draft a proposal of any kind? If so, on what basis did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: A minute ago I said I didn't have all the elements that are necessary for such an establishment, but on the basis of this order, I made a variant of a detachment that resembled a Territorial Defence detachment. It was a sort of detachment. There was a command -- there was a command, communications department, two or three companies, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While you were within the 3rd Corps Command, did you ever receive authorisation for that proposed formation?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: While I was there, no. No such formation was established.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at item 2, "Mobilisation preparations." A minute ago you said that in the 3rd Corps you and the service had no information according to which those foreigners were in the units or in the 3rd Corps. This first sentence says: "Replenish the El Mujahedin Detachment with foreign volunteers currently on the territory of the 3rd Corps zone of responsibility." What does this mean, in your opinion? Who are on the territory of the 3rd Corps zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Well, that's where they were. They were in that territory. So the detachment was to be formed of those men but not of 3rd Corps units. Men weren't supposed to be taken from 3rd Corps units. They weren't there. So these individuals were present in the territory of the 3rd Corps and the detachment was to be formed from those men who were not part of 3rd Corps units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, so as far as I have understood your answers, you were also involved in the mobilisation of men and of materiel for the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond units that you had or for the newly formed units. I'd like to ask you about the second sentence in this order. It says that the people mentioned should carry weapons and other materiel and other equipment with them that has already been issued to them. What does this order mean? How did you understand this order, when it says that these people should keep the weapons and other equipment which has already been issued to them?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: When we were establishing this formation, then I was told that these foreigners, these men, had their weapons. We didn't have weapons for our own men, let alone for them. So they carried these weapons with them. They'd obtain them from somewhere. They'd buy them. I don't know how or where. But they already had these weapons. And when it says "which has already been issued to them," I don't know whether these weapons had been issued to them on the basis of written documents or from their own warehouses, but that's what one writes down.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When a unit is formed on the base of an order and according to an establishment, is its -- is it its duty to provide your body with a report on its formation?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Usually one of us would go to the unit and spend two or three days there to assist them in forming the unit. There are always deadlines for all units -- for all units that were formed. In the case of all units that were formed, there is a sentence specifying that the commander of the unit should report on the completion of the task.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you or your colleagues at any time from your service go to that unit to assist them with establishing the unit? And while you were in the 3rd Corps, up until the beginning of November; did that unit at any time provide a report on its formation or, rather, on the process of forming that unit?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I and no one else from my body for organisation and mobilisation went there; otherwise, I would have been aware of that. As far as I know, we never received such a report about that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, tell me whether you in your records have a list of the commands of your subordinate units, have records on the commands of your subordinate units and did you know who the commander of that unit was or did you know who was in that unit until the time that you left the 3rd Corps at the beginning of November 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. There are documents containing information on all the units formed. There are records on officers from those units. It's normal to keep such records, and this was always done in -- in -- in the service. As we didn't receive a report that the unit had been formed, we weren't aware of any of the names of the men from that unit, so we weren't aware of its composition. We didn't even know who the commander of the unit was, let alone anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, when you look back to that period now, to the period during which you were involved in the affairs you have been testifying about here, could you tell me whether according to what you know about that period this detachment placed itself under the command of the corps up until the time that you left -- or by the time you left the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I said I didn't even receive a report on their formation, so until they are placed under the command of the 3rd Corps and there are written documents about this, this is not the case. So as far as I know, up until November 1993 this was a unit for which the 3rd Corps wasn't responsible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Poparic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Defence for Mr. Kubura, do you have any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions for this witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, we would like to distribute to all the parties the documents which we would like to touch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Poparic. I would just like to clarify a few issues with you. I don't think it should take too long. And, first of all, I'd like to go back to Prosecution Exhibit PX438. And that's the document authored by Enver Hadzihasanovic and dated 12th August 1993. Now, I believe you --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have an objection. My colleague just said that the document was drafted by Enver Hadzihasanovic. The witness spoke about certain other matters. In fact, perhaps one should specify that this document contains the name of Enver Hadzihasanovic, because this question does not arise from the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just -- I've looked at the list of exhibits that are proposed to be shown to this witness; P438 is on that list. But in addition to that, there are three new documents, and I would ask to address Your Honours on whether those documents can be shown to this witness, if my learned friend is going to show those documents to this witness, because our submission is that in accordance with Your Honours' previous ruling, which is very clear, these documents cannot be shown to this witness as part of the Prosecution's cross-examination. And I would, if they are going to be shown, ask to address Your Honours before that happens. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Before I give the floor to the Prosecution, there are two issues: Firstly, Defence counsel for General Hadzihasanovic claim that the document shown to the witness in which reference is made to General Hadzihasanovic, Defence counsel says that his name is contained in the document but he did not sign the document. That's the first issue. And secondly, Mr. Kubura's Defence note that there is a new document and Defence counsel would like to know whether this new document will be shown to the witness, since they claim that we, the Judges, have rendered a decision on new documents, and Defence counsel would like to know the legal basis on which the Prosecution would like to present this new document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I fully support the request made by Mr. Kubura's Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is a joint position, since both Defence teams agree on it. You may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. On the first point, I agree with my learned friend Residovic that the document has not been signed by Mr. Hadzihasanovic and that's not what I said. I said it was authored. And to be more careful, I should have said it appeared to be authored and -- but, you know, I just merely wanted to introduce the document to show it to the witness. I didn't want to suggest and I'm not giving evidence anyway. The document speaks for itself, and the witness already talked about that. And I won't touch that issue of who in fact signed it, because it wasn't signed. And the witness clearly said he did not know. He wasn't involved in that. He handed it over to some other department or some other person, and that's it. So I won't touch that. The second point, Your Honours, raised by Mr. Dixon, and supported by Mrs. Residovic, is these three new documents. In fact, listening to what the witness said in chief, I probably will only use the first 21s. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond And, Your Honours, in your ruling, in your oral ruling - I believe it was 29th November 2004 - you said that we could use or indeed tender new documents. And I can quote it: "To test the credibility of a witness or to refresh such a witness's memory." And you continue saying that: "These documents need not to be admitted at this time," so these can be new documents. And I quote again: "And which it had" - meaning the OTP - "in its possession before or after the presentation of its case." And you go on later on that same page - and, Your Honours, that's page 12.527 - to say that "If the documents are to be admitted, they can only carry limited value in a sense, as they relate to the credibility of the oral testimony or the refreshing process of the witness." So I believe, Your Honours, we are entitled to use it to test the credibility of the witness because he said a few quite straightforward points; namely, that the 3rd Corps didn't receive any information about these Mujahedin, the incorporation into the 3rd Corps, and I believe that both documents would -- would suggest otherwise. And I just wanted to show it to the witness and ask him whether he has to make any comments about it. Whether we are going to tender these documents, Your Honours, that's not yet decided. But to start with, we would like to mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to Defence counsel to hear the additional submissions they would like to make, I will reread the relevant paragraph of our oral decision dated the 29th of November, 2004. I will now reread it, and you can compare it with the transcript. And I'll read it out now. "It is the Chamber's opinion that the Prosecution may show in the course of their cross-examination any documents that have not already been admitted in order to test the credibility of the witness or to refresh the witness's memory. In each case, the Prosecution may present a document that hasn't already been admitted and which they had in their possession before or after the conclusion of its case. The Trial Chamber believes that when the Prosecution intends to present such a document, they must disclose this document to the Defence and inform them of their intention to disclose the document at least 24 hours before the witness for the Defence in question appears unless the Defence has belatedly provided the Prosecution with information that they need in order to prepare their cross-examination of the witness." That is what we decided with regard to new documents that had not been admitted into evidence but were in the possession of the Prosecution before or after the presentation of its case. We mentioned two cases in this decision, the credibility of the witness or refreshing the witness's memory. And in our decision, we added that it was necessary for the Prosecution to give the Defence at least 24 hours in advance the documents in question unless the Prosecution belatedly discovered that Defence counsel wanted to use a document. In such a case, the 24-hour notice could not be respected because they were made aware of the document too late. That was our decision. I will now give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to add two pieces of information. I called yesterday the Defence, both Defence teams, and informed them of my intention perhaps to use these documents. And the reason -- it's not exactly 24 hours. I think I called them around 1.00. But you have to in mind -- to keep in mind, Your Honours, that the 65 ter summaries are very, very brief. In fact, this witness, I think it's five lines, and it does not say that the witness disputes that these Mujahedin would be part of the -- the 3rd Corps. It just says he will testify about this document P438. But out of an abundance of caution, I thought this might be a relevant issue, so I called the Defence. We also disclosed both documents, Your Honours, in November of last year, so the Defence had the prior notice. And they could also discuss it with the witness yesterday, because they were alerted to these documents prior to the proofing session. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for this information about the necessity of informing 24 hours in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: There's no dispute over a few hours here or there on the part of the Defence. Our real issue, Your Honours, is that in Your Honours' decision the key wording as to whether a document can be shown is that it must test - and I underline "test" - the credibility of the witness or refresh his memory. And in our submission, neither of these documents do serve that purpose. Your Honour has the documents in front of Your Honours. Neither of these documents have anything whatsoever to do with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we continue, we will ask the witness to leave the courtroom. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom. Witness, you'll have to leave the courtroom for a while since there are certain procedural matters that we have to deal with. We will call you back into the courtroom as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence submits that in their view - but the Judges of course will confer about this - however, you must develop your argument. However, the said documents do not have the purpose of testing the credibility of the witness in your view. Can you expand on this? Because the Prosecutor says this is the purpose for which he's going to use the documents. You, however, assert the opposite. Could you please explain to us why you say this? And why you reject the arguments of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Both of these documents are ones which are entirely independent of this witness. These are not statements by the witness. These are not documents that the witness himself prepared. These are not proceedings. For example, the first document, an interview, that this witness was involved in. He didn't interview Mr. Durmis, for example. Nor did he prepare this list of the foreign citizens who left the El Mujahedin squad. These are documents that may relate to other witnesses. They may be documents that are referred to later. But they are documents which have no connection whatsoever to this witness. And we therefore submit there is no basis for challenging his credibility if it is not a document which he has some link to. If, on the other hand, the Prosecution had a -- a document which he had authored or a meeting that he was at where something different was done or said to what he has said in court before Your Honours, if there was an obvious contradiction in something he had said before and something he said today, then of course we would have no objection to that. Likewise, if he'd forgotten about something and a document that he had authored at the time was shown to him to try and refresh his memory, there would be no basis for the Defence to object. But in our view, the test is very strict. Your Honours have said that documents can only be shown for a limited purpose, and that must be to change the credibility of the witness. Credibility can only be challenged where something can be shown to be different to what the witness himself once did or once said and what he's said in his evidence today. Otherwise, Your Honour, we could be in a situation where -- where any possible document could be shown to a witness. A newspaper article from ten years ago which the witness has never read could be shown to him to seek to challenge his credibility. Your Honour, in our submission, that would be unfair. A witness can only be tested where he himself has been involved in something. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Otherwise, it's unfair to suggest to the witness that he's lied or that he hasn't told the -- the truth to this Court. In our view, the decision must be applied in that very strict manner. In addition to that, Your Honours, we -- we do agree with what my learned friends have said, that even if such a document were shown, that it has limited value because it purely goes to issues of credibility. But for it to have some value, in our submission, the best approach for Your Honours to adopt would be to always look very carefully at what documents are being shown and whether they truly can test the credibility of the witness or not. In our submission, these documents certainly cannot. They may well be documents that can be shown to other witnesses. In fact, the first document is one that the Defence team for Mr. Kubura has referred to in the past regarding the time when Mr. Durmis had left and was not involved in 7th Brigade -- 7th Brigade activities at all. But that's certainly not a matter which this witness can testify about. He wasn't involved in that interview, and it hasn't even been asked him whether he knows any of these individuals involved. So it may be that these documents arise later. But in respect of this particular witness, our submission is that there is no connection whatsoever to him or the testimony that he's given here today. Thank you, Your Honours, for the opportunity to make these submissions. We would also request that the Prosecution - the onus is on them, in our submission - seek to set out how they would challenge the credibility of this witness with -- with this document. In our submission, they can't do that on the face of these documents. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I fully accept the arguments put forward by my learned colleague Mr. Dixon, and I only wish to add that not only has the witness not drawn up these two documents; they have not been drawn up by the command of the 3rd Corps either. But also, neither of these documents is addressed to the witness or to the organ he was part of. Secondly, the first document clearly indicates that it is some sort of court record, and on our list of witnesses we also have judges. If the Prosecution wishes to use this document at all, it can perhaps introduce it, if you Judges so rule, when these witnesses arrive. Secondly, the way in which an accused's testimony can be treated in the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina cannot assist in any way when shown to this witness who has no knowledge of it. Secondly, these documents can in no way refresh the witness's memory, especially as the second document dates from 1994 and the witness said clearly that he left the 3rd Corps in early November 1993. Therefore, none of the strict elements in Your Honours' ruling can be met if such documents were to be shown to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Prosecution, after which we will retire to confer, I have to say to make everything clear that we have three documents. The first document is a record of an official interview with the accused Ramo Durmis, which has been translated into English. This is a record of an interview, and the document was signed by the accused, his counsel, and the judge. This interview was conducted in Zenica. And according to the first page of this document, one can see that it is dated the 26th of October, 1993. The second document is a list signed by Dr. Abu Haris on the 9th of February, 1994. The title of the document is "List of members of the El Mujahedin Detachment." The third document is a list of names several pages long, and apparently it was addressed to Sarajevo or sent to Sarajevo, and it was sent to the assistant to the minister of the public security service, and it contains a list of foreign citizens. We don't see the exact date on this document. We don't know how it was translated, how it came to be in the possession of the Prosecution, and why it was not disclosed to the Defence. I will now give the floor to the Defence, and after this the Judges will retire to confer. We shall do this only after we hear the final arguments of the Prosecution. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. In relation to the third document there, needs to be something said about the source. And I would need to go into private session but -- for that. But I'm not proposing to -- to use this document. So we -- we can just deal with the first two documents, if I may. Just in response to what my learned friend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. This means that the third document will not be used? We will not discuss it any more?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have less work to do, then. We only have go documents to deal with. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just in relation to what my learned friend Dixon -- Rodney Dixon said. The purpose of cross-examination is -- can be testing the credibility of -- of a witness. And I'm going to do that based on what he already testified in chief and what I anticipate he may be testifying in -- in cross-examination. And following up from a discussion we had the other day, Mr. Dixon and me, I reiterate: To test the credibility of a witness, I can put anything to him which is relevant. That's number one. And second, for which I have a good-faith basis to put it to him. That's the only restriction I have. And then the witness can deny it. It could be a newspaper article which was written about a relevant subject about which he testified. There does not need to be any more connection like that he signed something, he's mentioning an article. This type of information elements are normally used for a witness to tender a document to enhance his credibility, the authenticity, reliability of a document. But that's not cross-examination, in my submission, Your Honours. I need a good faith basis and it needs to be relevant. And I believe, Your Honours, both documents touch upon something the witness said before. He's, he says, an expert or has dealt with for 30 years, we have heard, about mobilisation, personnel issues, and in the relevant time frame of the 3rd Corps. I can certainly put to him that some people early 1994 left the 3rd Corps signed by the detachment commander, what it appears. And I can put it to him and say, "Here, you see the El Mujahedin Detachment has indeed been formed, as suggested by these two documents he discussed, P438 and 39," and let's see what he says. Perhaps he can add something useful. That's number one, the first document. And the second one, Mr. Durmis, he testified in front of this Court that he was a member of the 3rd Corps and the El Mujahed Battalion or Detachment. And I can direct you to -- to the second page of this Durmis record just after the middle. He says, and I quote: "At the time the crimes were committed, I was a member of the El Mujahedin Unit and I'm still a member of this unit." And that relates to July 1993, so that would contradict what the witness said that at this time there was no El Mujahedin Unit. And the witness, Mr. Durmis -- or the accused in that proceedings on page 4 at the end, last paragraph, also talks about the incorporation of this independent El Mujahedin Unit into the 3rd Corps of the BH army, again contradicting what the witness said or appeared to have said in examination-in-chief. So he, as a specialist in mobilisation, dealt with these issues. He would have an answer to these issues. And that's why I intend to use these two documents. Thank you, Mr. President. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is now 25 past 10.00. We will now have our break, as it is actually time for a break. We will have a break of some 20 to 25 minutes, and we will resume at 10.50, ten minutes to 11.00. Then we will tell you what our ruling is on this issue. Please rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall continue. And now the Chamber will hand down its ruling as to whether the Prosecution is to be allowed to use for purposes of testing the credibility of this witness two documents: One dated the 26th of October, 1993, which is in fact a record of an interview with the accused Ramo Durmis, dated 26th of October, 1993. The interview was conducted by a judge, an investigating judge of the High Court in Zenica. And the second document is a document compiled by Abu Haris, commander of the El Mujahedin Unit dated the 9th of February, 1994. The Trial Chamber has decided that these documents fall within the range of documents as to which the Chamber has already ruled, and the Chamber on the basis of this has decided that the documents may be used to test the credibility of the witness. The Chamber feels that these documents do fall within this category of documents, and this means that the Prosecution may use them for this purpose. We shall now ask the usher to bring the witness into the courtroom. Of course, the Defence will be able to return to this topic during their redirect. Did you wish to say something before the witness enters the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I just realised that one of the -- what I said before was not clearly translated or perhaps I misspoke. On page 35, lines 4 to 5, when I was talk about Mr. Durmis testifying in front of a court, it's not this Court here but it was, of course, the High Court in Zenica. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is why I mentioned in this oral decision of the Trial Chamber that the interview with Mr. Durmis was conducted before the investigating judge of the High Court in Zenica. Thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, the hearing has now resumed, and you will be questioned by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And good morning again. I would like first to ask you about a document you already talked about, and this is Prosecution Exhibit 438.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If that could be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the first question I wanted to ask you is on paragraph 2. On paragraph two, you talk about a mobilisation collection point. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Mobilisation collection point. This is the terrain where this unit is formed and comes into existence, and this is where it is located unless it is given another task. The mobilisation collection point is the location where a unit is formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And now, I believe you testified before the break - and please correct me if I'm wrong - that you -- the only thing you knew beforehand, before Mr. Mahmuljin approached you in relation to this to be formed unit was about the village of Mehurici. That's what you had known before. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew, as did most people, that there was a group of Arabs there, but not as soldiers. They were mostly in civilian clothing. They would enter the town of Zenica, where they mistreated people, did all sorts of things. But they did not exist as a unit, at least to my knowledge. I didn't know there was an armed unit of Arabs there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, incidentally, who in fact drafted this proposal? Was it you personally?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you also testified before that logistics was very limited or very scarce in -- in the 3rd Corps. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So that would be a big sacrifice if you used 3rd Corps -- if you propose to use 3rd Corps logistics for this El Mujahedin Unit, as you propose under item number 4.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a sentence that is usual in such documents. It refers to the overall logistics. But as to when it would enter into force and under what conditions would depend on the needs, on the requirements. This sentence "Logistics support will be regulated by the logistics services of the 3rd Corps," refers to something they can ask of us if we can provide it. Nothing more than that. Certainly the 3rd Corps did not have sufficient weapons or ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But that's what you suggested here, that these -- the El Mujahedin, if they were to be formed, would rely on the 3rd Corps logistics services.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Within the bounds of their possibilities. That's what's missing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, in fact, that's what was picked up -- thank you. In fact, that's what was picked up by the commander, Rasim Delic, in his letter of the next day. He, in fact, said, under item 3 - and perhaps you remember the second exhibit, P439 - that "Logistics support would indeed be provided by the 3rd Corps." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was based on our proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, before making the proposal, did you discuss that with the logistics commander, the assistant commander for logistics of the 3rd Corps, or anybody else, whether you had enough logistics support to deal with another unit, or did you consult with other people about that before making the proposal?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: No. No. As I said, this is a standard sentence where all units are informed, that they may ask of the corps command something that the corps command will provide provided it has it. It's also a question of time. This might happen in a year or two years. However, the corps command would be supposed to provide them with logistical support.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, incidentally, did the corps commander, Enver Hadzihasanovic, ever come to you and complain about your involvement or the involvement of Mr. Mahmuljin or in the creation of the El Mujahedin Unit, did he ever complain and say, "You can't do that." You know, "we don't have logistics"?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Any other discussions you had with Mr. Hadzihasanovic in relation to the El Mujahedin Unit or any other Mujahedin formations?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I don't recall. I don't think I ever had any such discussions. If I did, it would be with my immediate superior. However, I don't think we discussed this unit personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you were asked about the second document, again, P439, to comment on one of the sentences. And it's in the middle of the first page under item 2, "Mobilisation preparations." And it's the second sentence, and I quote it again: "These people keep the weapons and other equipment which has already been issued to them." And obviously this document comes from Rasim Delic. Now, do you know what -- if you know -- what the basis of information, the source of information was for Mr. Delic when he signed this letter?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: He probably had information according to which they had weapons. That is the only possible explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe you told us there may have -- they may have relied Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond on a warehouse to get these weapons. Can you tell us which warehouse you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Well, all units have their own warehouses. The 3rd Corps Command had depots from which certain equipment could be obtained. They certainly couldn't have requested any such equipment because we didn't have a sufficient amount. During that period of time, every third soldier had a weapon in the units that existed, so we weren't able to provide them with anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to the question put to the witness by my learned friend. And after I've checked page 14, line 13 [as interpreted], the witness did not say that they took weapons from certain warehouses. They -- it says that perhaps they had their own warehouses. So I don't think it's correct to suggest that the witness provided a different answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel says that the witness said that they had perhaps taken these weapons from their own warehouses, not from 3rd Corps warehouses, and he confirms that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has just confirmed what Defence counsel has said. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, my question was sufficiently broad. I said whether they relied on certain warehouses. I didn't ask whether they took it. But that's fine. The witness answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me go to a different issue, and that's the formation of the El Mujahedin Unit. So just to -- to be sure, did this process which we followed through these three documents, the one giving the authorisation of Mr. Mahmuljin to deal with the issue, that's P202; then 13 August 1993 document drafted by you, P438; and then the next day -- in fact, the same day he received the document, that's P439, when Mr. Delic basically ordered the formation. Did -- was a unit, El Mujahedin Unit, according to information actually formed in summer 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, that unit wasn't formed in the way we wanted it to be formed, according to these orders. They didn't have names, the establishment that had been determined, stamps that they were to use. These elements lacked while I was in the corps -- were lacking while I was in the corps command, so I don't think that the unit was formed in the way that we had planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So are you saying de facto the unit existed but they were lacking some formal criteria which were normally present when a unit was formed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I believe that it did exist and that they had their command, et cetera, but it did not want to be resubordinated to the corps command. They wanted -- well, I wouldn't say freedom, but they wanted to be assigned tasks from someone else, not from the corps command. That's the information I had at that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what's the basis for this information? Who gave you the information?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Information arrived, official information, unofficial information. People could observe the situation. We knew that there was a unit that was in existence, but we knew very little about them. Although, I was involved in operations, operational matters, I know that that unit was never issued orders for engagement. It wasn't assigned a zone of responsibility, et cetera. So for us, it didn't exist. We weren't aware officially of its existence, but we did know that it existed. But as to how many of them there were, et cetera, this is information we did not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like to -- to show you two documents which touch on this subject. And you may have a comment or two about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the witness could first be shown the document, the court record -- interview with the accused concerning Mr. Ramo Durmis dated 22nd [sic] October 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this appears to be a interview with a court. You see the -- the people present on -- on the cover page. What I'm interested in is on English page four, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President. Mr. President, it would perhaps be appropriate if my learned friend first asked the witness whether he knew the person in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The objection is sustained. It would perhaps be appropriate to find out whether the witness knows the person referred to in the document. In addition, there's an error in page 43, line six. It's the 26th of October. It's not the 22nd of October. But that's an error in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know the accused in this proceeding, meaning the proceeding before the High Court in Zenica, a person called Ramo Durmis, also known as Abu Jihad? And you can see even some more data on this person on the first page. Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I don't know this person personally; although, this is an address in the vicinity of my home. I don't know him personally, but I have heard about him. I think he was involved in a murder or in -- in stealing something. I think he was a criminal. That's when I heard about him. But I don't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me direct you to the last paragraph of page four. In English and in the B/C/S original - B/C/S meaning Serbo-Croatian - it's on page 4. And it's the fourth paragraph from the bottom, and it starts: "Napitanje," [phoen] in your language. And I'll read it out in -- in English, Your Honours. "In answer to a question asked, the accused said" - apparently a quote - "About two and a half months ago, this independent El Mujahedin Unit was incorporated into the 3rd Corps of the BH army. Until then, it had not been formally part of that formation but had operated independently and carried out the riskiest operations with great success in agreement with the 3rd Corps." Now, what can you tell about that? Here Mr. Durmis now claims that this unit was indeed formed and was incorporated into the 3rd Corps. Can you -- can you help us about -- about that? Do you agree with it or you disagree?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I don't know what duties he performed there. I don't know where he obtained information according to which they were under the 3rd Corps Command. I don't believe that this is correct, and I don't know where he obtained this information from, according to which they were subordinated to the 3rd Corps. There is no document that would support this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, this person - and you see that on -- on page 2 - the end of the page in the English version, and in your version it's after the middle of page 2, he says - and I quote him - "I was a member of the 7th Muslim Brigade unit until April 1993 and I did a lot as a participant in its operations. After that, our unit, which is now called El Mujahedin, was separated from the said brigade and has since operated as an independent detachment," and so on. End of quote. So this person, in fact, was in that unit, so he -- he should know.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I don't believe these allegations, not at all. I don't even believe that in the 7th Muslim Brigade there were men with Arab names. Perhaps this man was a member of the 7th. But in that detachment, there were quite a few local men. Perhaps they did separate and join those Arabs. That's a possibility. But that they did that with our agreement, I wouldn't agree with that. I would have had to draft such an order and provide it to the commander so that he could certify it, an order according to which a group from one unit was to be transferred to another unit. Perhaps this was done, but if it was done, it was without our agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But doesn't that suggest what Mr. Durmis says was in fact in accordance with the process which had been initiated by you and Mr. Mahmuljin that a El Mujahedin unit was to be formed? And here we have somebody on the ground who in fact performed that. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I agree, but as far as the dates are concerned, we obviously don't agree. These dates that were before the commencement of the case. Perhaps they were preparing for the formation of that unit. I am making assumptions. When they had a sufficient number of men, et cetera, perhaps they took the initiative to form such a unit. I really don't know though.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just incidentally, going back to the first document, P438. In the middle of the page, it said - and I quote - what you drafted, "Given the need to organise and make use of foreign volunteers as well as their written request to the 3rd Corps Command." What written request was that? "Their," I take it meaning these people who wanted to be part of 3rd Corps. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I haven't understood you very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In that paragraph I quoted - and that's from the 12th August 1993 document, Exhibit 438, in the middle it says -- I believe it's the other one, the document dated Zenica 12th August 1993. You had drafted it. It says: "Given the need to organise and make use of foreign volunteers, as well as their written request to the 3rd Corps Command." Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What written request was that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I haven't seen this document. It's obviously Mr. Mahmuljin who had the document, and at the time they probably requested to form a unit and be placed under someone's command. I assume that that is the document. But I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me go to the second document I wanted to show you, suggesting that indeed a El Mujahedin detachment was formed, as you have suggested. And that's the one-page document dated 9th February 1994. Now, let me ask you first, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I haven't seen this document before, but I can see the date, the 9th of February, 1994, a list of men who left the detachment. Perhaps after I had left the corps command in November 1993 there were such men who had these names, but this is the first time I've seen such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, do you know the purported author of this document, an Emir Dr. Abu Haris?
