utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know any other individual which is listed in this document, points 1 to 17?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I said that while I was in the corps command we never received a list of men with Arab names. This is really the first time I've seen this. And naturally, I don't know any of the men included in this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the heading of it, it says: "Army of Republic BiH 3rd Corps squad or detachment El Mujahedin." That suggests that indeed an El Mujahedin squad within the 3rd Corps of the Army of the -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina existed, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: It might have existed after my departure, between November and February 1994. It might have been established in that period and put under command, but not while I was there. While I was there, this unit or detachment did not exist. As to what happened later, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, after you had sent off your proposal of 12th August 1993 and after your command had received Mr. Delic's order in which, incidentally, I think he sets a deadline for the completion by 31st of August, did anybody complain with you that the order of Mr. Delic has not been implemented? Did you ever hear of any complaints to you personally or -- or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: No. I really never heard anyone say that the order had not been implemented. I knew that it had not been established, but as to whether anyone complained about that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the basis of your knowledge that it's not been established is because you have not seen any documents?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We never received any document about the implementation of this order, and we should have received it. When a unit was established, we had further obligations. For example, we made all the stamps that the unit had and issued it to the unit. While I was, there this was not done. Therefore, I draw the conclusion that until November 1993, this detachment did not exist officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me ask you just two more questions. The first one: I understand that your office, your department had personnel information on all the units that were part of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: It was supposed to have all this information. It wasn't always updated, but we did have lists of members for most of the units. Perhaps 70 per cent of these lists were correct. Because there was a lot of coming and going, a big turnover, so the lists were not reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you ever hear of a massacre occurring on the 24th of April, 1993 in and around the village of Miletici? Have you ever heard of a massacre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't deal with operative matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question falls completely outside the context of the examination-in-chief. The witness did not testify about this, but the witness has already answered that he never dealt with such matters. So perhaps my objection is needless, but it's outside the scope of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. President, I should have asked -- I should have asked leave. I would like to ask this person, who admittedly was in charge or in this personnel department, whether anybody ever asked him to provide information about individuals who might have been involved in -- in massacres. It's about the indictment, which says that there were no investigations, no prosecutions done in relation to these incidents. And I would like him to provide information whether somebody approached him, since he was in the personnel department of the 3rd Corps. That's the line of questioning - it will be brief - I wanted to launch into.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is completely clear even to us civilians that the organisation and mobilisation service has nothing to do either with combat operations or investigations into certain events. Therefore, I think there is absolutely no basis for putting this question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence says first that this question falls outside the scope of the examination-in-chief, and therefore leave must be asked of the Trial Chamber to put this question. Secondly, the Defence also says that the witness dealt exclusively with issues of mobilisation, not operative matters, as he stated at the very outset. So what use is it to put such a question at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if -- if I might just reiterate. Because he was in the personnel department, me as a Prosecutor, investigator, I may address him and ask him for information about the possible units who were involved in these -- in these massacres. And if he doesn't know, if he hasn't dealt with that, that's fine. But I believe I'm entitled to -- to ask this question, with your leave obviously, which I have forgotten about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By a majority of the votes, the Chamber has decided that you may ask the witness whether within the scope of his duties as a person in charge of personnel he had any knowledge in connection with any requests or any investigations or requests for information. You may put the question to the witness and we shall see what he says. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You've heard what the President said, and I'm asking you about possible investigations into two events. One is Miletici, the 24th of April, 1993; and one is the villages of Maline and Bikosi, on the 8th of June, 1993. Now, were you or, if you know, somebody else from your department ever approached to provide information concerning a possible investigation or prosecution into these events by military authorities, civilian authorities, security authorities? Are you aware of any requests like that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I never saw anything like this, nor did anyone ever ask me personally about anything like that. I can't say whether they asked that of anyone else, but I believe not, because I would have known about it. I learned about this first case only much later, when I was performing a new duty in the civilian protection. That was the first time I even heard of that first incident. Nobody ever asked this of me, and I believe no one asked any of the people working with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that relates to -- to both these incidents I mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And my last question - and, Your Honours, I take it I need again leave for that question. I would like to ask him whether his office or himself had ever issued certificates in relation to soldiers of the 3rd Corps in order that a court can determine whether the appropriate jurisdiction was a military one or a civilian one. Because that's an issue which may become relevant about the, again, Ramo Durmis case. There is some information that certificates were issued, and so I think he would be a witness who could tell us whether he, as part of the 3rd Corps Command in charge of personnel, ever dealt with this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the Judges hand down a decision, I would like to hear from the Defence. The Prosecutor wishes to ask the witness whether he, within the scope of his administrative duties, in the personnel department, within he was ever asked to issue certificates for soldiers of the 3rd Corps and these certificates were issued for the purpose of being sent to military or judicial authorities. This was what you wanted to ask; is that correct, Mr. Waespi? Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's for you to decide. I, again, feel that this falls outside the scope of the examination-in-chief because we did not ask about any court proceedings. If the witness can answer whether he issued any certificates or not, we leave that to Your Honours to decide whether this question can be put or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have no objection to this question being asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before saying that the decision has been reached by a majority of votes, I have to say that this question does not relate to the credibility of the witness. It falls outside the scope of credibility. However, we will approve it because it is in the interests of justice and in the interests of establishing the truth. On this basis, we will give you leave to put this question and we will give leave to the witness to answer it, of course, as this is a question falling within the scope of the witness's sphere of activity at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Colonel, I understand you are still a -- a colonel -- occasionally obviously it's an issue whether a person, an accused soldier, and tried before a military court or a civilian court. Did your department ever issue certificates on behalf of soldiers for the purpose or -- of that determination, whether he's indeed a soldier and for what unit, so that the judges can decide jurisdictional issues? Do you remember whether that was ever done?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: We did issue certificates that someone is a member of the army on the basis of our records. In this certificate, at the bottom the purpose of the document always had to be stated. I do not recall that we ever issued a document saying that somebody was a member of the army for the purposes of some sort of legal proceedings before a court or because of an investigation. I don't remember ever issuing a certificate for this purpose. The certificates we issued were usually for the purpose of resolving questions of status and of social welfare. I don't recall them ever being issued for purposes of legal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know whether lower units issued certificates like that, the personnel department of lower units?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, units could issue such certificates and use their own stamp on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, I appreciate your answers. I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Poparic, my learned friend showed you again some documents that I also showed you. And when asked whether in relation to the proposal you drew up, whether you ever discovered this with Commander Hadzihasanovic, and as far as I recall, you said you never discussed it with him?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And also, in connection as to whether General Hadzihasanovic ever expressed disagreement with what you had done, I ask you now: Was Commander Hadzihasanovic a professional soldier?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a professional soldier yourself, if a person receives authorisation from your superior command, can you then challenge this authorisation?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it normal for a superior command to issue orders to subordinate units and so subordinate individuals?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: It's their right, but it would be proper to inform the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you had received an order from the Supreme Command Staff dated the 13th of August establishing the El Mujahedin and that you acted in accordance with that order and drew up, to the best of your knowledge, a proposal for the establishment, although this was your not duty. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to or was anyone else able to say they would not implement this part of the order?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you abide by your previous testimony that approval for such an establishment was never received by the 3rd Corps or you personally while you were in the command of the 3rd Command -- Corps?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: We could only draw up proposals, but the order could only be issued by the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While you were in the 3rd Corps, did you ever receive this from the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to the questions put to you by my learned friend when he showed you some documents, please tell me: Do you have any knowledge of any legal proceedings, especially criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: No. This did not fall within my sphere of competence, and I really don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about what rights and position an accused has in criminal proceedings when defending himself, and is he duty-bound to tell the truth? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that your units could issue certain documents confirming membership, the membership of certain persons in their unit. Was this a general right or were these situations that had to be ordered by the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: We're talking about certificates of membership? These certificates could be issued by the units because one couldn't travel 150-kilometres to reach the corps command, so the units were able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you personally know whether at any time whether any unit issued a certificate to a member for the purpose of legal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: No, I have no information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, tell me, were you in a position to monitor the certificates issued by various units in the area where the 3rd Corps was active? Were you in a position to verify these certificates?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: That was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any military regulations which would instruct a unit to send such a certificate for your authorisation before it was issued?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as this second document is concerned, the one that you said you had never seen, and you also said that it never arrived in the 3rd Corps before you left. And the date also shows that it was issued in February 1994. Could you please have another look at this document. Can you see a stamp of any kind on this document, a stamp that would belong to the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: There is no such stamp. Tell me, were you at any time familiar with any of the names listed here?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: No. I had never heard any of these names before, nor did I know these Arabs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether any of the individuals listed here actually existed? Did these people actually exist?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I read this out, could you tell me whether these are names of people Saif from Tunis, Baif from Tunis, Sain Jihad, someone from Pakistan, someone from Palestine, someone from Libya? Are these the names of people?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: It's obvious that these are just nicknames. These are false names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. The Prosecution wants to object.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The point being the witness said he never heard any of these names before, so I thought there was no purpose to go into that, unless Defence proves he's an expert in the Arabic language and name-building.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just wanted to ask the witness whether as a normal man from Bosnia-Herzegovina he thought that these were names. I read the names of these individuals out, but it's obvious that what we can see in this list has nothing to do with names. That is what the witness has confirmed. Here it mentions individuals from Bahrain, from Palestine, et cetera, et cetera. There are no names referred to here. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I object to Mrs. Residovic testifying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Perhaps there's a translation error. We're trying to see things clearly now. Defence counsel has presented this document and want to know whether the names listed in the document mean anything to the witness, and Defence counsel wants to know whether these are in fact names. Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, regardless of the Prosecution's position, in your opinion, are these actually names in the document? What is your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This -- these are obviously nicknames based on the origin. If someone's name or surname is Tunis or Maghreb [phoen] or Suriname, et cetera, then obviously these are the countries of their origin. These aren't names.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for providing this clarification which was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We only have a few questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Poparic, my learned friend has already shown you the statement made by Ramo Durmis, the statement given to the High Court in Zenica on the 26th of October, 1993. And we can see that he signed this statement in the presence of the investigating judge and the public prosecutor. You have read that document.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend, Mr. Waespi, today quoted from the statement of Ramo Durmis according to which he was in the 7th Muslim Brigade up until April 1993. You heard the question put to you by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend also asked you about the El Mujahed Unit. And if I have understood this correctly and made a correct note of it, you said that there were local men in that unit too; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to hear this answer, Mr. President because there might be some confusion, on page 45, line 12 of the transcript, and I believe this answer has clarified matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: My second question -- my next question has to do with the document shown to you by the Prosecution. February 1994 is the date of the document. At that time, you weren't in the 3rd Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, do you know -- are you aware of the fact that in February 1994 in Travnik the 7th Muslim Battalion -- Brigade no longer existed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: That's what I heard. I know that once I had left, it continued to exist for a while and then it was subordinated or resubordinated to a brigade. I wasn't working at the time, so I don't know what happened to the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the 27th Brigade had been formed by that time and that all the men and the entire 1st Battalion from the then-7th Muslim Brigade moved to the newly formed 27th Brigade? That was towards the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: When I was leaving the corps command, the 27th was formed and the 37th was being disbanded, which never really came to life. But that was the period during which I was already in the process of leaving the corps, so I really didn't know that the battalion from the 7th Muslim had joined the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd just like to correct something in the transcript. It says "in February 1994 the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade in Travnik no longer existed." [as interpreted]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I just have a few questions to clarify certain things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that your service had to prepare stamps; is that correct? You had to prepare stamps for units?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. For all the units formed that were subordinated to the 3rd Corps, for all those units we had to produce these military stamps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as you can remember, as of August, when the issue of creating this El Mujahedin Unit was raised, did your service make or produce any stamps for this unit?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no, we didn't produce any such stamps, because we quite simply didn't even know whether it had been formed. Usually once a report is received stating that a unit has been established, then the unit is provided with the relevant stamps. As we did not have such information on such a detachment, I don't believe that we ever made any stamps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you said that you received -- that you would receive a document saying that it had been -- saying that the unit had been formed, and in such a case you would send them stamps.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you also said that you left the 3rd Corps in November 1993 to go to the Main Staff, which was involved in protecting civilians. And as far as I have understood, on the base of the transcript, on the base of your testimony, you returned to the 3rd Corps later. When did you return? In which year and in which month?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I didn't return to the 3rd Corps, but after one year had passed, I returned to the ABiH, to the Main Staff and I performed the same duties there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you were in the Main Staff, which was based in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: In Kakanj. There was a command post there too, so I was in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there was a command post in Kakanj. Very well. Thank you for having provided this clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good morning, witness. I have two questions to put to you in relation to what you told us about the El Mujahedin Unit and its relationship with the or absence of relationships with the 3rd Corps. You said before the break that -- and after the break also that officially the El Mujahedin Unit did not exist as far as the 3rd Corps was concerned. You knew as a fact that there was a unit, but officially it did not exist. And you also said it had -- it was not a unit for which the 3rd Corps was responsible. That was the last remark you made before the break. Now, assuming that what you say is correct, I want you to help me in the first place in understanding a document that is dated from September 1993. If I follow your reasoning, your remarks, there are questions I have with relation -- in relation to this document. And I want to show it to you. It is document P440. And maybe you could help me in understanding the meaning of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll place the document on the ELMO so that everyone can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: We have discussed this document with other witnesses in the past, but I'm interested in the language of the document in relation to what your testimony of today is. As you may know, this is a document of the 7th -- the 6th of September, 1993. It originates from the 3rd Corps. And on the bottom at the left hand there are initials "SM/HA." Do you know who "SM" might be?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Usually the person who drafted the document would place his initials there, such as "SM." But other initials than those of the operations officers who worked on packet communications. This would be taken to the commander to be signed and the person who drafted the document was probably one of the operations officers in the 3rd Corps. As far as the contents of the document are concerned, my personal opinion, although I wasn't involved in these affairs, is that this was an attempt made by the commander to put that detachment to use. In September it had probably already been formed, but we weren't informed of the fact, and this was probably an attempt made by the commander to place it under his command or to place it under someone's command. Whether -- as to whether this was done, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I'll put the very first question I should have put to you: Have you seen this document before or is it new to you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: It's the first time I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Now, when another document was shown to you - and this is document 438 - there were initials at the left bottom side saying "PM." And you said, "These are my initials. I am the document -- I have drafted this document." And so, therefore, I put to you the question: Do you recognize who drafted the document in P440? Is SM the person who drafted the document? It's not of enormous importance, but I'm just satisfying my curiosity.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I can't remember who had those initials. Because there were a lot of operations officers and we didn't have that much contact. They performed their duties. We performed ours. So right now I can't remember who that person was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Do you recognize the -- the initials of the -- of the person who signed the document, on the right-hand side at the bottom across the stamp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you show the witness the document again. Let's place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: This isn't my commander's signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, have a look at the contents. And I'll ask you a question on -- on language. Just read the document in its entirety. You've seen it? Well, let me quote the --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: -- the sentence of the order given. It is: "To resubordinate the El Mujahed independent detachment to the Bosnian Krajina OG Command for the forthcoming combat activities, in accordance with the plan of Bosnian Krajina OG." In view of what you said this morning about the El Mujahedin not being a part of the 3rd Corps, I would like to ask you what in this context of your testimony means "to resubordinate a unit"? How do I have to understand that you -- how do you resubordinate a unit that is not part of your -- your own corps? That is my question to you.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: In September, there was probably a form of contact. This is what I assume. I had no direct knowledge. But I assume there was contact with this detachment that was being formed. There was contact between the detachment and the corps command. And I assume that this was an attempt to finally use this unit in accordance with our plans. In this particular case, in accordance with the plan of the Bosnian Krajina operational group. I think that is what is at stake. As to whether this was actually carried out, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. The logical question I have is: Can you resubordinate a unit that is not part of your own corps, your own brigade, your own unit? What is your opinion on that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: I can only repeat what I have just said. Theoretically speaking, that is not possible. But since they had already received an order in August to work on the formation, well, I'm not sure but perhaps they were supposed to become companies, platoons, et cetera, but I assume that in September they could have been used and perhaps there was contact and there was an attempt to put that unit to use and to ensure that it was part of the 3rd Corps. I can't see any other possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did you in your position or did you not follow the -- the developments in the field, in terms of military operations? Were you informed about military operations going on in your position?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: No. No. My service dealt with the organisation of the army, the creation of units, replenishing the units, with manpower, but it was the Chief of Staff and the operations officers who planned combat activities. We did not have information about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does the Prosecution wish to put any further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, just two small issue, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you could have a look again at P440, the document Your Honour Judge Swart showed to you. [Microphone not activated] And if you look at the signature block where it says "commander." Do you agree with me that -- Thank you. Sorry. If you can look at the signature block where it says "commander." Do you agree with me that it says or it appears to say "Za Komandanta," meaning "for the commander"?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. So somebody was signing on behalf of the commander somebody was acting as a deputy. This is, if I may say, the signature of Dzemal Merdan. That's his initials there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the last issue is -- I know you left in 1993 and I believe November 1993, but have you heard of an order which was issued from the High Command in 1995 to destroy the stamps of the Mujahedin Unit? Have you ever heard of that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: No. No. I've never heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And my last question is: The issue of the El Mujahedin Unit and the way it was formalised or not. You said there were no stamps issued. But it's correct that they were assigned the official numbers, the T-number, the five-digit T-number, and also a four-digit military number in your language - it's called "Broj vojne jedinice" - that was assigned to -- to that unit?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: No. Yes, they got this in the order, the order on the formation of the unit. That's where it says where -- the VJ number, the number of the military unit is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may take the floor further.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Poparic, previously we saw this order issued by the staff of the Supreme Command. I will not put the document before you again. But in the provisions it says that "This newly established unit will be in the mobilisation plan of the 3rd Corps. Does this mean that the Supreme Command staff wanted this unit to be part of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Obviously yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You testified that they did not do everything they were supposed to do according to the order. Tell me, did you personally mobilise this unit?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As this order was issued by the Supreme Command Staff and was the formal document whereby this unit came into existence, tell me, was the command of the 3rd Corps duty-bound to try to implement this order?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: We forwarded this order and we expected them to call upon us as the proper professional persons to assist them in establishing their unit. No one from the corps, at least not from my service, was ever requested to go and assist them in this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you testified previously when looking at this document, the document says that the proposal for the establishment should be delivered to the Supreme Command Staff, and you testified that you had done this. Is it usual, in view of the fact that the Judge showed you the document of the 6th of September, for other organs of the corps to attempt to implement the order that came from the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Would you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you carried out your part of the obligation stemming from the order of the Supreme Command by proposing the establishment.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question is as follows: Would it be normal for other organs in the corps to do what you did and attempt to implement the order of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that they would have to try. But whether they actually did anything specific, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, just objection to these questions which requires the witness to go beyond his corps. He cannot possibly discuss other corps. And also, these questions are very difficult to answer or to assess for Your Honours. Is it usual or is it normal? I believe that's -- that's too vague for -- for a question to -- to ask, especially also in re-examination and when it's about clarification of -- of open issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood the question put by the Defence correctly, it is as follows: Pursuant to the questions put by His Honour about the document issued in September, the counsel asked the witness whether it would be usual or normal for someone else besides the witness to respond to the order issued by the Supreme Command. Was that the purport of your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise if my question was not sufficiently clear. As His Honour Judge Swart showed a document and the witness said that he felt it was an attempt by the commander to use the units, on the basis of this I wanted to ask the question of the witness as to whether it would be normal if a unit had been established for other parts of the corps, including the commander, to try to implement this order by wishing to use the unit. The witness previously said that he carried out his part of the order. I think it was not too difficult for the witness because he answered each one of my questions. Everyone to whom the order referred attempted to implement it. Thank you. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But from the military viewpoint, the witness should answer the question. Can you do that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said previously, I believe that other organs, because a unit was being established which was supposed to have certain basic military things the same as other units had, I believe that the operation men tried, that the logistics men tried. I believe they all tried to help those people. But I don't have any knowledge about it and I personally never went there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Prosecution, I wish to say the following: In answer to this question, witness said that it seemed normal to him that other organs of the 3rd Corps should work on this issue. I now give the floor to the Prosecution in order to conclude this discussion. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The witness answered, in fact, the question Defence should have asked him: Do you have any knowledge whether other organs of the corps did something? That would have been the proper question. But just to ask: Is it normal that something happens? That just -- just doesn't help us any further. But the witness answered. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Defence may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions for this witness. I wish to thank my learned friend because it's always useful to learn how questions should be put. I thank him for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As for the admittance of documents, which documents do you wish to tender?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no documents to tender because we have shown the witness only documents that have already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Sir, do you wish to tender any documents, for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, at least make a definite or a specific status for these documents. We don't wish to tender the two documents I have discussed with the witness because the relevant parts have been read out on the record and the witness answered it. But we would like to mark it for identification. So perhaps in a -- at a later stage we can go back to these documents if -- if the need arises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Interpretation] Just a minute. There is a problem with the interpretation because we're not receiving any right now. Mr. Registrar, could you please check the problem. It seems that everything is functioning now. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] New documents can be used only for strictly limited purposes. I see no basis to have these documents marked for identification now. For general use in future proceedings, the Prosecution will be able to do this in their rebuttal, if they wish to tender these documents. Only if they wish to use them for a specific purpose to test the credibility of the witness, then they must do so now, but not have them marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honours. It's, I think, a matter which all the parties agree on that these documents are not to be regarded as evidence in the case. Your Honours' ruling was very clear on this matter that these documents cannot be used to strengthen the Prosecution evidence against the accused or in any way to deal with the individual criminal responsibility of the accused. They have been shown merely for the purposes of testing the witness's credibility. And in -- in that regard, we do wish to have it placed on record that the only area where credibility was allegedly tested by the Prosecution was on the existence or not of the El Mujahed Unit. In addition to that, Your Honours, we -- we do note that the witness was not able to identify anything in these documents, certainly, for example, with the second document, the list of foreign citizens. He was not able to identify anyone on that list or the person who had purportedly prepared this document. So in our submission, we have reference to these documents on the record by the Prosecution for the purposes of cross-examination, and the matter need not be taken any further at this stage. There's no need to in any way mark these documents. They can be left as documents referred on the record. And Your Honours are able to assess the witness's answers for the purposes of -- of credibility. That, in our submission, would accord with the decisions Your Honours have given today and the earlier decision. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Would the Prosecution respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I agree with most what Mr. -- Mr. Dixon said; although, he had a little broad concept of anything related to individual criminal responsibility. Anyway, we don't regard it as evidence. I agree with him. We don't tender it. It's a merely technical processing of these documents that they receive a number so perhaps later if a similar witness appears - and there are still many to come - or perhaps in rebuttal or reopening, whatever, that it's easier for us to trace these documents. There is nothing sinister about giving it a number. It's not evidence; we agree with it. But usually in other proceedings I think they receive a technical number so we can -- we can easier trace them. That's the only purpose for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber will consider this technical aspect which the Prosecution has now put forward. Sir, as far as you are concerned, your testimony is over now. We thank you for coming and contributing to the establishing of the truth. You have responded to all the questions put to you, both by the Defence and the Prosecution as well as by the Trial Chamber. The parties showed you documents. This is something that is necessary, as you know. You held high-ranking posts in the army. You are a retired colonel. So it was evidence that you by your knowledge were able to contribute to the interpretation and understanding of these documents. Thank you for this. The Trial Chamber extends its best wishes to you and wishes you a safe return home, and we wish you a happy retirement. I will now ask the usher to take you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is now time for our break. It is already 12.30. Are the witnesses ready?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. The witness is ready. But in order not to interrupt the beginning of the witness's testimony, we have two documents, 0419 and 0879, left over from yesterday, which had not been translated into English. We have now submitted the translations, so may we regulate these two questions before the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Mundis. What have you to say about these two documents which had not been translated and now have been translated and you have had a chance to review them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We have indeed, Mr. President. We have no objection to those documents, 419 and 879, being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. May these documents be admitted into evidence. MR. REGISTRAR [Realtime transcript read in error "MS. RESIDOVIC"]: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. These two documents will be admitted into the record as DH419, and its translation as DH419/E; and the other document will be marked DH879, and its translation into English will be DH879/E. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have now heard the final numbers assigned to these documents. It is now 25 to 1.00. We shall resume at around five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Usher, could you call the witness into the courtroom, please. There's a slight error in the transcript, line 8, page 74. Mr. Registrar mentions the numbers -- the exhibit numbers for documents, not Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I would first like to make sure that you are receiving the interpretation of what I am saying. If so, please say that you can hear and understand me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will shortly ask you to take the solemn declaration, but I'd first like you to tell me your first and last names, your date of birth, and your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Zivko Sakib. I was born on the 25th of June, 1956 in Tesanj in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you currently employed? And if so, what is your job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am now retired. I am a teacher of defence and security matters by profession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, did you hold a position of any kind? And if you were in the army, which unit were you in and what rank did you hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In 1992, I was a member of the Supreme Command Staff of the ABiH, up until the 20th of November. And as of the 20th of November, 1992 until the 20th of August, 1993, I was a member of the 3rd Corps Command of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified before an international or national court about the events that took place in your country in 1992 and 1993, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Defence, who will start with their examination-in-chief, which will continue tomorrow since we only have 45 minutes before the end of the hearing, I would like to provide you with some information. You will first have to answer the questions that will be put to you by Defence counsel, who will be conducting their examination-in-chief. The questions they put to you will always be phrased in a neutral manner so as not to suggest any answers to you. Once this stage has been completed - and it should not take too long since another witness has been scheduled for the tomorrow - the Prosecution, who are to your right, will put a series of questions to you which will have a direct bearing on the questions put to you by the Defence. Once this stage has been completed, Defence counsel may ask you additional questions. The three Judges sitting before you may also at any point in time put questions to you in order to clarify some of the answers that you have provided to the parties or to ask you about the documents that they are already familiar with, since they have been admitted into evidence. I would also like to point out that, as you have solemnly declared to speak the truth, you should not give false testimony. As you are well aware, false testimony constitutes an offence, and there is another provision contained in our Rules: If you believe that an answer you provide to a question might cause you problems at a subsequent date, since the answer contains information that might be used against you, you may refuse to answer the question. The Chamber may, in such circumstances, compel you to answer the question but grants you a form of immunity. I am pointing this out, but it is purely theoretical since this case -- or such a case has never arisen to date. If you feel that a question is complicated, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it, since, as you know -- or perhaps you're not aware of the fact -- we don't have any written documents that concern you. We do not know what your answers will be in advance, so it is your testimony that will be transcribed. It will appear on the monitor that you have before you. Your testimony will be transcribed and the transcript is in English. This is the procedure we will be following, and I'm sure that things will run very smoothly. As we have 45 minutes left at our disposal, you will have to return tomorrow for the cross-examination. I will now give the floor to the Defence, who will commence with their examination-in-chief. Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I would also like to point out that as we speak the same language, you might want to answer the questions I put to you immediately, but as the Presiding Judge has already said, there is a monitor that we all have in front of us and we can follow everything that is said on this monitor. It is necessary for my questions and your answers to be interpreted, so I would be grateful if you could make a brief pause after I have put my question to you and then answer the question so that everyone can follow our exchanges. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were a professor of defence by profession. Tell me whether before the war you were involved in affairs that were related to defence. If so, when did you have a rank of any kind?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: Yes. I completed the school for reserve officers in Tuzla, the infantry section. I was then engaged in the military in the Hadzici Municipal Staff and in the Ilidza Municipal Staff afterwards, and for the last nine years in the Sarajevo Regional Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What duties did you have in the Regional Staff of the Sarajevo Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: I was involved -- I worked as an operations and intelligence officer in the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a rank at the time?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: Yes. I held the rank of captain.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the JNA attack on Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 6th of April, did you remain in that position or did you assume any other duties?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: When the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina started, I placed myself at the disposal of the Regional Staff in Sarajevo. Afterwards, on that very same day I moved to the Supreme Command Staff of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ziko, can you tell me what sort of duties you performed in the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: From the 8th of April, I worked as an officer -- as a liaison officer. I was involved for contact between the ABiH and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Afterwards?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: After the OG one in the Supreme Command Staff was formed, I was appointed as the chief for intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you remain in that position until you moved to the 3rd Corps Command?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: No. On the 20th of August, I was returned to the Supreme Command Staff as an officer for operations and my task was to monitor the situation in the Zenica region.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given the duties you had that involved monitoring the situation in the Zenica region, were you aware of the reason for which Mr. Enver Hadzihasanovic left Sarajevo and went to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: Yes. I knew the reason, since we were both in the Supreme Command Staff, and I knew what Mr. Hadzihasanovic's task was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what his task was.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: At the time, Mr. Hadzihasanovic's task was to act with the 3rd Corps forces and units on Igman, to lift the blockade of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After Mr. Hadzihasanovic had left Sarajevo with that task and after he had gone to the Zenica area, did you in the Supreme Command Staff receive a report of any kind on the situation in that area? And if you did, what information did you have after Mr. Hadzihasanovic had left Sarajevo, that had been encircled?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: Since I was a member of the Supreme Command Staff and I monitored the situation in the Zenica area, all written reports forwarded by Mr. Hadzihasanovic were reports that I could see. All the written reports he sent to the Supreme Command Staff. I could see them and I could read them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what sort of a situation Mr. Enver Hadzihasanovic found and can you tell us about the extent to which it was possible for him to carry out the task that he had been assigned.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: Since I was in Sarajevo, in the Supreme Command Staff we didn't have a very clear idea of the situation in the Zenica area. We were in Sarajevo; that was encircled.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ziko, you don't have to wait for your answer to be fully transcribed before answering.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: We didn't have a clear view of the situation and units in the Zenica area, and Mr. Hadzihasanovic forwarded a report according to which there were no troops there, no organised formations with which he could do anything as far as carrying out his initial task was concerned. And his task was to lift the blockade of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ziko, tell me whether you know whether at the time Mr. Hadzihasanovic was issued another order; and if so, what kind of order was he issued?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: Since we carried out analysis of all the information obtained from the Zenica region and Mr. Hadzihasanovic confirmed that information at a joint meeting of the Supreme Command Staff a decision was taken according to which Mr. Hadzihasanovic and a group of officers should establish a corps, train the members, and he was charged with this task.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that later you moved over to the 3rd Corps. Tell me, why and when did you leave Sarajevo and what sort of order was there with regard to you leaving the town?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: Given the report from Mr. Hadzihasanovic according to which there were no combat groups in Zenica that could carry out the task that he had been assigned, a group of officers -- or rather, nine officers in the Supreme Command Staff were assigned the task to go to Zenica and place themselves at the disposal of Mr. Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think you have already said that you left.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: Since I was involved operational affairs and I monitored the situation in the area of Zenica, it was logical for me to be one of the officers who would go there and continue with my work as an operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What duties were you assigned in the 3rd Corps when you arrived there at the end of November?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: I was assigned duplicates in the operations and training organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us about the tasks you had been set and what sort of attitude did Commander Hadzihasanovic have towards the body that you were assigned to?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: Commander -- the commander of the corps -- or a commander of a corps and of larger units knows what an operations unit is and what an operations and training body is. It's the commander's right hand. It's the commander's brain. So in this sense, at the very beginning he tried to establish a good operations and training organ that would assist him with his work, a body that would make good proposals for his further work. When assigned to the operations and training organ, we started organising an operations centre, a communications centre, and all other elements of importance in an operations and training organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what did you have at your disposal initially and did you know what the situation was on the ground?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: In view of the fact that I was an operations officer, I had an erroneous picture of the situation in the Zenica region. When I arrived in the corps command, we found only empty offices without any technical equipment, such as an operations and training organ needs for its work. We had no technical equipment, no maps, and we received this from the Zenica Regional Staff as well as some auxiliary communications equipment, what they had at their disposal at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please: What was your attitude toward establishing your function toward the subordinate and superior commands? Did you take any measures in this respect? And if so, what measures?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: As I had arrived from the Supreme Command Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I knew what the method of work was in the Supreme Command Staff. We did something similar in the 3rd Corps, and this link functioned from the very beginning. We found very different officers in Zenica, various officers, at the disposal for the corps formation. We had to train them to work in the operations centre so that they could take duty shifts and contribute to our work. We had special problems in the lower-level units, in the brigades and the battalions, where there were no officers capable of responding to the duty facing them. It was our obligation to train these lower-ranking officers or at least give them instructions in order for their work to be as good as possible. At the outset, we did this through an order and through suggestions about the way they could carry out their activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was the method of work of the training centre? Were there any office hours? Or did you work in some other way?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: The operations centre worked round the clock. All the officers in the 3rd Corps Command were in the command, and at any point in time, whenever they were needed, they were at the disposal of the staff of the 3rd Corps and, therefore, at the disposal of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a method of reporting set up in your organ, or, rather, in the corps?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: Through the order and instructions we gave to the officers working on operations, we suggested how they should do their job. The first problem we came across which had a great influence on the work of the 3rd Corps Command was the lack of communications equipment. At that time, we tried to solve this problem through all other methods of conveying information, including the simplest, by courier or, if needed, by telephone if possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Ziko, did you only issue orders, or did you monitor the implementation of these orders? In other words, did your method of work include direct insight into the situation on the ground or were you just in your operations organ offices working there?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: All the information that arose in the area of the corps command arrived in the operations centre. This was the only centre where this information was gathered. The duty team that was set up for every working day of 24 hours and the presence of one of the operations officers of the operations and training organ of the 3rd Corps, which was obligatory, they were all there to analyse the information and to alert whoever needed to be alerted, if necessary, or at that time we drew up proposals for orders for the removal of shortcomings and for the taking of measures that were necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may the witness be shown some documents I would like to use. I would ask the usher to distribute the documents, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These problems in establishing the method of reporting and the work of the operations and training organ -- or rather, the operations centre, were they solved quickly or did efforts have to be made over a longer period of time to solve them?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: Although our efforts were directed at removing the shortcomings as soon as possible in order to provide good quality information to the 3rd Corps Command and thereby the commander, our efforts did not yield any results for a long time. It would often happen that officers who had already been trained or at least informed as to how they should do the work of the operations organ would be appointed to other positions and their duties would be continued by someone who had no idea as to how they should do this work.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ziko, this set of documents, would you please look at the document under tab 2, and it bears the number 1194; and another document, P271, and tell me whether these are documents illustrating the situation you have just testified about, that is, your efforts and the situation as regards reporting to the 3rd Corps by the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: Yes. These are precisely those documents that were drawn up in June. There had been other orders previously asking for the same elements as are found in this order, both in the first order and in the request for the delivery of combat reports, that is, document 0181118.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, now: When you received information from the subordinate commands, what was your duty? Was it your duty then to submit this report to someone? And was there any time frame, if you had such an obligation, within which you had to carry it out?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: The obligation of the operations and training organ and the team on duty on that day was when these reports arrived, whatever they were like - and they differed a lot, both by the method of working and the way in which they were drafted - to study these documents, and if there was any change in the first line of defence or anything else of importance to the operations organ, to enter this information into the maps. The other elements that were of importance to other officers from the staff organ could be forwarded to these, and then they would continue working in accordance with the information. Only matters of a high significance were conveyed to the Chief of Staff, who was our immediate superior, and it was his duty if he felt it necessary to inform the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who compiled the report for the Supreme -- for the staff of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: This was done by operations officers from the operations and training organ. The duty of the organ was to submit a daily report once a day with the situation in the area of responsibility of the corps and, if need be, to submit several interim reports, especially when there were HVO attacks on BiH army units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: As you have just said that you analysed the reports that arrived and that the duty officer, the operations officer decided on what was important and had to be conveyed to the Chief of Staff, how many such reports in your estimation arrived at -- to the corps commander's desk?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: These reports which we had to submit to the Supreme Command were rarely seen by Mr. Hadzihasanovic, but his name was in the signature of all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ziko, does this mean that a piece of information that you thought important might be forwarded to the Supreme Command Staff without your commander receiving this information either from you or from the Chief of Staff? Was such a situation possible?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: As the area of responsibility of the corps was very large and the situation on the ground was chaotic, it was the commander's duty to be frequently absent from his command post in order to influence the situation by his presence and improve it. Therefore, we could not fail to forward these reports waiting for the commander to come back. Anyone who was around would sign these reports, the Chief of Staff, the duty team in the operations centre, and we operations officers in the operations and training organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So these were reports sent to the Supreme Command Staff. Tell me, please: The reports that the subordinate units were duty-bound to submit to the 3rd Corps and which arrived in your operations centre, did the commander regularly read these reports, or, if not, approximately how many such reports and how did they reach the commander? Who evaluated whether they should be sent on to the commander?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: As I have just said, all the reports arriving in the operations centre were analysed by the operations team and these reports, such as they were - sometimes very dry and sometimes vague - they were all collected and the most responsible officer who was in the corps command at the time would be informed of them if we thought that the information was significant for the course of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that in the commander's absence you had an obligation toward the superior command. Anyone in the operations centre or in the command would sign these reports. If a report was sent by packet communications to another organ and the whole would be signed -- or, rather, the name in the signature line would be Commander Enver Hadzihasanovic, would this mean that the commander had actually previously seen, approved, and signed the document?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: No. Bearing in mind the situation and the habit people had of seeing the commander as the only authority in relation to the lower units and the duty of the commander to send reports, we could use only his name. So his name was always there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, in this time period, you said that you sent instructions, orders, and so on and so forth. While you were there, that is, until the 20th of August, 1993, did you go out on the ground, and what was your role on the ground? What tasks did you carry out in the field?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: The operations and training organ of the corps staff, apart from collecting information, analysing it, also had to check the situation on the ground. Very often we would receive information from a third organ, or whoever, that the situation in the units was not what it was reported to be in their reports. Whenever we received such information, we would inform the Chief of Staff and propose to him and thus to the commander that we should go out on the ground and to see for ourselves what the composition of the command was, how they were operating, what the situation in the units was, and everything else of importance for us for planning the use of the units. And in view of our obligations, I think that each unit was visited at least two or three times and some of them more frequently if they asked for assistance or if we noticed that they were not complying with the orders we had sent them regarding the work of the operations organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ziko, tell me, you in the operations and training organ, did you have the duty to make a note in some of your documents and maps of the strength, composition of units in the territory of the corps?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of our main tasks, so that on the basis of the situation in the corps we could allocate them at the appropriate zone of responsibility. This would be based on their strength and on the materiel and equipment they had.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you received such information from units and included that information in official documents of the corps command, did you have any information on the existence of units composed of foreigners? Or, rather, did you have information that in some 3rd Corps units there were foreigners from Afro-Asian countries. While you were in the 3rd Corps did you have such information and did you include such information in your documents or rather the maps?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: We didn't have such information and I personally didn't have such information, and since I was one of the officers that worked on those maps and monitored the situation in the field, monitored the situation in units as well, during that period of time I had no contact with foreigners nor did I see any foreigners in those units. I would have had to be aware of such a situation. If there had been any such individuals, we would have had to include information of them in our orders and such a person would have been duty-bound to provide us reports on the situation and the unit concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you have already said that you visited all units two or three times and some units were visited even more frequently, does this mean that you personally went into the field?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to controlling the situation, we would also inspect corps units, and I participated in such inspections so I can claim with full responsibility what I have just said.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When inspecting or visiting units or when assisting the commands of subordinate units, did you on any occasion see foreigners who were members of those units or, rather, did some commanders during that period of time, from November to August, boast or complain about the presence of foreigners in their units which were used in combat?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: No, I had no such information. And since I was frequently in contact with the commanders of all units and it was their duty when they came to the corps to provide other information not included in reports, given that I had such contact with them, I can say that I had no such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ziko, you spoke about the difficult situation in the territory of the 3rd Corps. For this reason, the commander often -- was often absent from the command. Tell me whether there was a period during which the commander spent a long period of time outside the command in Zenica. And if so, could you explain the situation?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: Given the situation in the corps, the commander was very frequently absent for various reasons. And since those units and parts of units that he had contact with performed better, he believed it was important for him to visit other units with a group of officers. This took a long time. It was also his duty to go to Sarajevo, to the Supreme Command Staff. And when the battlefield Zepce was opened up, he was absent for a lengthy period of time. So at the forward command post he didn't have good information or, rather, information that would arrive in the 3rd Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned combat activity and the situation in Zepce, could you please tell me as an officer who was involved in combat operations, what importance were those fights for Zepce. Of what importance was the fighting around Zepce your corps and for the situation throughout the free territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: I'd like to make two or three distinctions. As far as my presence in the 3rd Corps Command is concerned, when I arrived in the 3rd Corps Command, there was only one enemy that we had: The Chetniks -- or, rather, the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor who were facing us. This was particularly evident when they were breaking up our forces or routing our forces in Jajce and expelling the population towards Central Bosnia. That's the first thing I wanted to mention. But secondly, after HVO representatives started provoking members, hindering the movement of our units, and rotating them, and in the operations and training organ we had to provide daily information on the movement of units to the HVO. The third thing I'd like to point out is that there was a conflict from April up until the time I left. There was open fighting, and the commander made efforts to calm the tension in that part of the battlefield to avoid conflicts of any kind with the HVO so that we could deal with our other objectives and to make it easier for the men at the front lines facing the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor. When the HVO and Chetnik forces joined up in the Zepce area, they disarmed the 319th Brigade in Zepce. They killed some of the troops. They arrested the others. And this situation compounded the situation in the 3rd Corps Command. The commander believed that his presence was essential in that area. And in the Golubinje sector we established a forward command post with a minimum of officers and a communication centre so that we could stop our members from fleeing. They were fleeing, just like the civilians. We wanted to organise a defence in that area. That was the most difficult period for Mr. Hadzihasanovic because the situation was difficult. There was no materiel or technical equipment. The Supreme Command Staff had requested that part of the units be sent to Igman and then Igman, which is above Sarajevo, fell. And given the lack of materiel and technical equipment and men for rotation, the situation was extremely difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ziko, could you have a look at the following documents. One o documents is from the command of the 3rd Corps, 1296 -- DH1296 forwarded to the Supreme Command Staff. And then have a look at DH1298. It's also a 3rd Corps document, dated the 11th of July, 1993. And could you please tell me whether these documents and document P599, which is also a document from the 3rd Corps Command dated the 30th of June, 1993, could you please tell me something about these documents and say whether these documents are documents that give a good view of the situation, the situation that prevailed at the time of the intensive fighting in Zepce.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB ZIKO
utterances.text: Yes. These are some of the reports we would forward to the Supreme Command Staff, to our superior command. It reflects the actual situation. And given the request we had of the corps command, it reflects such a situation. And in these requests you can see the situation in those periods and you can see the extreme difficulties Mr. Hadzihasanovic was in. He wanted assistance. He did not just want to be asked to undertake things that weren't realistic and weren't possible.
